sources.title: Role of AMP-activated protein kinase in mechanism of metformin action
sources.design: Preclinical: rat hepatocyte and L6 myotube experiments with pharmacological AMPK inhibition
sources.population: Rat hepatocytes and L6 myotubes (preclinical, non-clinical)
sources.preview: Foundational preclinical study showing metformin activates AMPK in rat hepatocytes and L6 myotubes; a pharmacological AMPK inhibitor blocked metformin's suppression of hepatic glucose production, suggesting AMPK was required. Metformin activated AMPK, reduced acetyl-CoA carboxylase activity, and suppressed lipogenic enzyme expression. Findings are from preclinical cell experiments.

sources.title: Metformin inhibits hepatic gluconeogenesis in mice independently of the LKB1/AMPK pathway via a decrease in hepatic energy state
sources.design: Preclinical: hepatocyte-specific AMPKalpha1/alpha2 double-knockout mice and LKB1-deficient mouse experiments
sources.population: Mice with liver-specific AMPK knockout or LKB1 deficiency (preclinical, non-clinical)
sources.preview: Showed that metformin still inhibited hepatic glucose production in hepatocyte-specific AMPKalpha1/alpha2 double-knockout mice and LKB1-deficient mice; gluconeogenesis suppression was actually amplified in knockout animals compared with wild-type, correlating with reduced hepatic ATP content rather than AMPK activity. Demonstrated an AMPK-independent, energy-state mechanism for gluconeogenesis inhibition. All findings are from preclinical mouse models.

sources.title: Metformin inhibits mitochondrial adaptations to aerobic exercise training in older adults
sources.design: Randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of supervised aerobic exercise training
sources.population: Healthy older adults aged 65 years and older undergoing aerobic exercise training
sources.preview: In a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial, metformin attenuated skeletal muscle mitochondrial biogenesis in healthy older adults undergoing aerobic exercise training compared with placebo; markers of mitochondrial content including citrate synthase activity and electron transport chain components increased with exercise plus placebo but were blunted with exercise plus metformin. These are human trial data in older adults without diabetes.

sources.title: Metformin Inhibits Advanced Glycation End Products-Induced Inflammatory Response in Murine Macrophages Partly through AMPK Activation and RAGE/NFkB Pathway Suppression
sources.design: Preclinical: murine bone marrow-derived macrophage cell experiments with advanced glycation end products stimulation
sources.preview: Metformin pretreatment suppressed advanced glycation end product-induced inflammatory responses in murine macrophages through AMPK activation and RAGE/NF-kB pathway suppression. The pro-inflammatory M1 marker CD86 was reduced and the anti-inflammatory M2 marker CD206 was elevated; pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1beta, IL-6 and TNF-alpha were reduced while anti-inflammatory IL-10 increased. All findings are from preclinical murine macrophage experiments.

sources.title: Immune-mediated antitumor effect by type 2 diabetes drug, metformin
sources.design: Preclinical: solid-tumor mouse model experiments with CD8-positive T cell analysis and immunodeficient mouse controls
sources.population: Immunocompetent and immunodeficient mice bearing solid tumors (preclinical, non-clinical)
sources.preview: In solid-tumor mouse models, metformin promoted immune-mediated tumor rejection by protecting CD8-positive tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes from exhaustion; metformin treatment increased the number and function of tumor-infiltrating CD8-positive T cells, enhanced cytokine production including interferon-gamma, and maintained an effector memory phenotype. In immunodeficient mice lacking T cells, the antitumor effect was abolished, demonstrating that the benefit required intact T cell immunity rather than a direct anti-proliferative effect. AMPK activation was proposed as the metabolic mechanism supporting T cell function. All findings are from preclinical mouse experiments.

sources.title: Metformin Suppresses Both PD-L1 Expression in Cancer Cells and Cancer-Induced PD-1 Expression in Immune Cells to Promote Antitumor Immunity
sources.design: Preclinical: cancer cell-line experiments and mouse xenograft models
sources.population: Cancer cell lines and mouse xenograft models (preclinical, non-clinical)
sources.preview: Metformin suppressed PD-L1 expression in cancer cells through AMPK-dependent inhibition of AKT-mediated beta-catenin phosphorylation, reducing transcription of the CD274 gene encoding PD-L1; metformin also restored ubiquitin-dependent degradation of PD-1 in natural killer and T cells. Combined effects reduced tumor immune evasion and suppressed xenograft growth in vivo. All findings are from preclinical cell-line and mouse experiments.

sources.title: Effective breast cancer combination therapy targeting BACH1 and mitochondrial metabolism
sources.design: Preclinical: cancer cell-line experiments and patient-derived xenograft mouse models
sources.population: Triple-negative breast cancer cell lines and patient-derived xenograft mouse models (preclinical, non-clinical)
sources.preview: Identified BACH1 as a transcriptional repressor of mitochondrial electron transport chain genes in triple-negative breast cancer. Depleting BACH1 or accelerating its degradation with hemin shifted energy metabolism from glycolysis toward the tricarboxylic acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, sensitizing cancer cells to metformin. The BACH1-targeting plus metformin combination suppressed tumor growth in cell lines and patient-derived xenograft models. All findings are from preclinical cell-line and xenograft experiments.

originalAction.text: Metformin's established glucose-lowering action combines reduced glucose production by the liver, reduced intestinal glucose absorption and improved uptake and use of glucose by tissues. It improves insulin sensitivity without stimulating insulin secretion. Repurposing research asks whether changes in cellular energy sensing, growth signals and the handling of damaged cellular material can be useful beyond diabetes. AMPK is an energy-sensing enzyme, while mTOR signaling helps regulate protein production and cell growth; altering these systems can have different consequences in infected cells, tumors and healthy muscle. The evidence below distinguishes effects measured in experimental models from proposed explanations and from clinical outcomes, because demonstrating a pathway change does not establish that a treatment helps patients.

pathways.title: Insulin sensitivity and growth signaling
pathways.text: Improving insulin sensitivity is part of metformin's established action in diabetes. In cancer repurposing, reducing insulin-related growth stimulation is one proposed route to benefit. The MA.32 breast-cancer trial measured changes in insulin, weight and other metabolic factors, but its clinical report did not show improved invasive disease-free survival. These findings distinguish a measured metabolic effect from an unconfirmed anticancer benefit.

pathways.title: AMPK, mTOR and the balance between energy use and growth
pathways.text: AMPK activation and reduced mTOR signaling provide a rationale for changing cell growth and protein production. In myeloma cell lines and mouse xenografts, metformin activated AMPK, suppressed mTORC1 and mTORC2 signaling, and was associated with autophagy, cell-cycle arrest and reduced tumor growth. In viral infection, suppression of host-cell protein production is a proposed explanation for reduced SARS-CoV-2 replication; the COVID-OUT nasal-swab study measured viral RNA rather than directly proving that mTOR mediated the reduction in viral RNA. The same growth-related pathways also matter in healthy tissue: mTORC1 supports muscle growth, and metformin reduced muscle gains during resistance training in the MASTERS trial. A mechanism that appears useful in one setting can therefore work against the intended outcome in another. The same restraint of mTOR-related growth signals extends to aerobic-exercise adaptations: in a randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of supervised aerobic exercise training in healthy older adults aged 65 years and older, metformin attenuated skeletal muscle mitochondrial biogenesis compared with placebo, with markers of mitochondrial content increasing in the exercise-plus-placebo group but not the exercise-plus-metformin group. Together, the resistance-training and aerobic-exercise trials show that metformin blunts both muscle mass gains and mitochondrial adaptations to exercise in older adults, an important consideration for individuals who rely on exercise training for health.

pathways.title: Autophagy and mitochondrial stress
pathways.text: Autophagy is the cell's process for recycling cellular material. In Parkinson's disease cell and mouse models, metformin was associated with AMPK activation and autophagy, less mitochondrial oxidative stress and reduced accumulation of alpha-synuclein. Blocking AMPK or autophagy weakened protection in toxin-injured cells, supporting a contribution from these pathways within that model. Inhibitor specificity, the experimental exposure and the difference between toxin injury and human disease limit translation; these experiments do not establish that metformin slows Parkinson's disease in people.

pathways.title: Complex I inhibition and energy sensing
pathways.text: Two preclinical studies in cells and isolated mitochondria show that metformin inhibits complex I of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, the enzyme that initiates electron transfer during cellular respiration. In intact hepatoma cells, 50 micromolar metformin produced time-dependent inhibition of complex I activity, reducing glutamate oxidation by 13 percent after 24 hours and 30 percent after 60 hours; succinate oxidation, which enters at complex II, was unaffected, confirming selectivity for complex I. In a complementary study using isolated rat hepatocytes, inhibition of cell respiration by metformin occurred only in intact cells and not in permeabilized cells or isolated mitochondria, demonstrating that the mechanism requires an indirect, cell-mediated signaling step rather than direct drug contact with the enzyme. In isolated sub-mitochondrial particles, half-maximal inhibition required approximately 79 mM, far above therapeutic plasma concentrations, while the effect appeared at 50 micromolar in intact cells, consistent with intracellular drug accumulation. Reduced flux through complex I lowers cellular ATP production and is proposed to be one upstream trigger for the AMPK activation described in other pathway studies. These are preclinical findings from cell lines, isolated hepatocytes, and sub-cellular fractions; they do not establish the concentrations, tissue distribution, or extent of complex I inhibition during therapeutic metformin treatment in people.

pathways.title: Mitochondrial glycerophosphate dehydrogenase inhibition and hepatic redox
pathways.text: A 2014 preclinical study in rodent models showed that metformin inhibits mitochondrial glycerophosphate dehydrogenase (mGPD), an enzyme on the inner mitochondrial membrane that links glycerol metabolism to the electron transport chain. Inhibiting mGPD allows NADH to accumulate in the cytoplasm, increasing the cytosolic redox state; at the same time, the mitochondrial redox state decreases. This altered hepatocellular redox balance reduces the conversion of lactate and glycerol into gluconeogenic substrates, thereby suppressing hepatic glucose production. Acute and chronic low-dose metformin treatment reduced endogenous glucose production in rodents while producing the predicted redox changes in both cytosolic and mitochondrial compartments. When hepatic mGPD was knocked down in rats using antisense oligonucleotides, the animals developed a phenotype resembling chronic metformin treatment, and metformin could no longer increase cytosolic redox, lower plasma glucose, or inhibit endogenous glucose production. These findings were confirmed in whole-body mGPD knockout mice. Because mGPD inhibition suppresses gluconeogenesis through a redox mechanism that does not require AMPK activation, this pathway is proposed as an alternative or complementary route to complex I inhibition for how metformin reduces hepatic glucose output. All findings reported here are from preclinical rat and mouse models; this study does not establish the degree of mGPD inhibition during therapeutic metformin treatment in people.

pathways.title: Gut microbiome shifts and intestinal action
pathways.text: Metformin accumulates in intestinal tissues at concentrations exceeding plasma levels and has well-documented effects on gut microbiota composition. In a 4-month randomized double-blind trial in individuals with treatment-naive type 2 diabetes, metformin produced strong shifts in gut microbiome composition compared with placebo. Transfer of fecal samples from metformin-treated donors to germ-free mice improved glucose tolerance in the recipient animals, suggesting that at least some of the antidiabetic effect is mediated through microbiota changes. Metformin affected pathways with shared biological functions in species from two bacterial phyla, and many metformin-regulated genes encoded metalloproteins or metal transporters. A separate analysis of 784 human gut metagenomes showed that metformin treatment can confound gut microbiome signatures attributed to type 2 diabetes itself, because the two conditions have distinct but overlapping microbial signatures. Metformin was associated with increased short-chain fatty acid production, proposed as a beneficial mechanism, but also with a relative increase in Escherichia species abundance, which may underlie some intestinal adverse effects. A gut-restricted mechanism of action is supported by delayed-release metformin formulation data: a formulation targeting the distal small intestine lowered plasma glucose and enhanced fasting and postprandial GLP-1 and PYY secretion despite approximately 28% lower systemic bioavailability compared with immediate-release metformin. The maintained glucose-lowering effect at lower plasma drug levels, combined with enhanced gut hormone release, provides evidence that metformin acts directly on intestinal tissue and not solely through portal delivery to the liver.

pathways.title: GDF15 induction and appetite suppression
pathways.text: Growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) is a stress-response cytokine that reduces food intake and body weight by acting on a brain-stem-restricted receptor called GDNF family receptor alpha-like (GFRAL). Two preclinical studies showed that GDF15 is an important mediator of metformin's effects on body weight and energy balance. In mouse models, oral metformin elevated circulating GDF15, with the increase in GDF15 expression predominantly in the distal intestine and kidney. Metformin prevented weight gain on a high-fat diet in wild-type mice but not in mice lacking GDF15 or its receptor GFRAL; a GFRAL-antagonist antibody reversed the weight-reducing effect of metformin in obese mice, confirming that GDF15 signaling through GFRAL is required for metformin to influence body weight. Notably, metformin retained its glucose-lowering action in the absence of GDF15 signaling, indicating that glucose control and body weight effects involve separate mechanisms. A complementary preclinical study found that metformin stimulates GDF15 secretion in primary mouse hepatocytes by increasing expression of the transcription factors ATF4 and CHOP/DDIT3; in GDF15 null mice, metformin did not reduce food intake, body mass, or fasting insulin. In patients with type 2 diabetes taking metformin, higher serum GDF15 concentrations were associated with weight loss, an observational human association consistent with the mouse mechanistic data. All mechanistic data are from preclinical cell and animal experiments; the human association is observational and cannot establish causation.

pathways.title: Lactate elevation and lactic acidosis risk
pathways.text: Metformin inhibits complex I of the mitochondrial respiratory chain, reducing the rate at which the mitochondria oxidize NADH. This slows the conversion of lactate to pyruvate by altering the cytosolic NADH/NAD+ balance, shifting equilibrium toward lactate production. Lactate concentrations therefore tend to rise in tissues where metformin is active, raising the theoretical concern that this could cause lactic acidosis. The clinical significance of this pharmacological effect has been extensively studied. A Cochrane systematic review pooled 347 comparative trials and cohort studies covering 70,490 patient-years of metformin use; it found no cases of fatal or nonfatal lactic acidosis in metformin-treated patients, and the upper limit for the true incidence was 4.3 cases per 100,000 patient-years versus 5.4 in comparison groups. Mean lactate levels and net change from baseline did not differ between metformin and non-metformin antihyperglycemic treatments. A community-based cohort study subsequently examined the risk of acidosis across the full range of kidney function and found that metformin use was associated with acidosis only at eGFR below 30 mL/min per 1.73 m2. At eGFR between 30 and 44 mL/min per 1.73 m2, the association was not statistically significant in either the primary or replication cohort, supporting cautious use of metformin at eGFR at least 30 mL/min per 1.73 m2. The clinical conclusion is that metformin does increase lactate at a biochemical level through complex I inhibition, but this rarely translates into clinical lactic acidosis in patients who are otherwise healthy and have adequate kidney function; risk is substantially higher when kidney impairment prevents metformin clearance.

pathways.title: AMP accumulation, AMPK activation, and dependence on AMPK for gluconeogenesis inhibition
pathways.text: A proposed mechanistic chain connects metformin's inhibition of complex I to downstream AMPK activation through changes in adenine nucleotide concentrations. When complex I is inhibited, ATP synthesis slows. A preclinical study using 31P-NMR spectroscopy in isolated perfused rat hearts showed that metformin (at 10 mM) increased cytosolic free AMP concentration over time; AMPK activity and phosphorylation of its substrate acetyl-CoA carboxylase were elevated only after the rise in cytosolic free AMP, consistent with free AMP acting as the upstream trigger. Notably, total AMP content and the total AMP/ATP ratio did not increase, indicating that it is the metabolically active free cytosolic AMP rather than total AMP that signals to AMPK. A review of metformin mechanism of action in diabetes and cancer described this chain further: complex I inhibition leads to defective cAMP and protein kinase A signaling in response to glucagon, contributing to suppression of gluconeogenesis; AMPK activation, while not strictly required for the glucose-lowering effect of metformin, confers additional insulin sensitivity mainly by modulating lipid metabolism. Whether AMPK is strictly required for metformin's glucose-lowering effect has been tested across two key preclinical studies with different conclusions. A 2001 study in rat hepatocytes and L6 myotubes found that metformin activated AMPK and that a pharmacological AMPK inhibitor blocked metformin's suppression of hepatic glucose production, suggesting AMPK was necessary for the gluconeogenesis-inhibiting effect. A 2010 study using hepatocyte-specific AMPKalpha1/alpha2 double-knockout mice found that metformin still inhibited hepatic glucose production in the knockout animals; LKB1-deficient mice, which cannot activate AMPK through the canonical upstream kinase, also retained a full metformin response, with gluconeogenesis suppression actually amplified compared with wild-type animals. In that study, the gluconeogenesis-suppressing effect correlated with decreased hepatic ATP content rather than AMPK activation, supporting a direct energy-state mechanism independent of the kinase. These preclinical data indicate that AMPK activation is a real consequence of metformin's energy perturbation and may confer metabolic benefits in insulin-sensitive tissues, but that AMPK-independent mechanisms including direct effects on hepatic energy state and the mGPD pathway contribute to gluconeogenesis inhibition; the degree of AMPK dependence in humans has not been established.

pathways.title: NF-kB suppression via AMPK, MDR1/P-gp chemoresistance reversal, and macrophage polarization
pathways.text: AMPK activation by metformin has been linked to suppression of NF-kB-driven transcription in cell-line experiments. A preclinical study in adriamycin-resistant MCF-7 breast cancer cells showed that metformin activated AMPK and reduced MDR1 (P-glycoprotein) expression by inhibiting NF-kB transcriptional activity and CREB phosphorylation. Overexpression of the p65 subunit of NF-kB increased MDR1 promoter activity, and metformin attenuated this increase; siRNA knockdown of AMPK attenuated metformin-mediated MDR1 inhibition, confirming that the effect depends on AMPK. A dominant-negative mutant of AMPK reversed metformin-mediated inhibition of both MDR1 expression and CREB phosphorylation. Separately, a review of metformin mechanism notes that AMPK activation modulates lipid metabolism, which connects to lipogenesis regulation. Metformin also modulates macrophage polarization through AMPK and NF-kB-linked pathways. A preclinical study in murine bone marrow-derived macrophages found that metformin suppressed inflammatory responses induced by advanced glycation end products through AMPK activation and suppression of RAGE and NF-kB signaling; the pro-inflammatory M1 marker CD86 was reduced while the anti-inflammatory M2 marker CD206 was elevated, and pro-inflammatory cytokines IL-1beta, IL-6 and TNF-alpha were reduced while anti-inflammatory IL-10 increased. All findings in this section are from preclinical cell-line and murine macrophage experiments and do not establish anti-inflammatory clinical benefit.

pathways.title: Anti-tumor immunity: CD8-positive T cell exhaustion rescue and PD-L1 suppression
pathways.text: Metformin has been shown in preclinical models to influence antitumor immune responses through direct effects on CD8-positive cytotoxic T cells and through suppression of the PD-L1 immune checkpoint ligand in cancer cells. A 2015 preclinical study in solid-tumor mouse models showed that metformin promoted immune-mediated tumor rejection by protecting CD8-positive tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes from exhaustion. Metformin treatment increased the number and function of tumor-infiltrating CD8-positive T cells, enhanced their production of cytokines including interferon-gamma, and maintained a multifunctional effector memory phenotype. In immunodeficient mice lacking T cells, the antitumor effect of metformin was abolished, confirming that the observed antitumor activity in immunocompetent mice required intact T cell immunity rather than a direct anti-proliferative effect on tumor cells; AMPK activation in T cells is proposed to support metabolic fitness in the energy-poor tumor microenvironment. A 2024 preclinical study in cancer cell-line and mouse xenograft models found that metformin suppresses PD-L1 expression in cancer cells through AMPK-dependent inhibition of AKT-mediated beta-catenin phosphorylation, reducing transcription of the CD274 gene that encodes PD-L1; metformin also enhanced ubiquitin-dependent degradation of PD-1 in natural killer and T cells. These complementary mechanisms - supporting CD8-positive T cell persistence and reducing tumor-cell expression of PD-L1 - are proposed as routes by which metformin could enhance antitumor immunity in combination with established immunotherapies. All findings are from preclinical mouse and cell-line experiments and do not establish clinical immunotherapy benefit.

pathways.title: BACH1, cancer energy metabolism reprogramming, and combination strategies
pathways.text: Cancer cells frequently reprogram energy metabolism toward aerobic glycolysis partly by suppressing mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, which may limit their sensitivity to agents that target mitochondrial metabolism. The transcription factor BACH1 contributes to this metabolic reprogramming in some cancers by suppressing expression of genes encoding electron transport chain components, reducing cancer cells' dependence on mitochondrial function. A 2019 Nature study showed that in triple-negative breast cancer, BACH1 protein levels and transcriptional activity suppressed mitochondrial metabolism; depleting BACH1 or accelerating its degradation using the heme-oxygenase inducer hemin shifted energy metabolism from glycolysis toward the tricarboxylic acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, increasing cellular dependence on the mitochondrial function that metformin impairs. The combination of BACH1 targeting with metformin suppressed tumor growth in both cancer cell-line models and patient-derived xenograft experiments, while neither agent alone showed the same degree of efficacy, suggesting a synthetic metabolic vulnerability created by the combination. These preclinical data support the cancer-hallmark concept that metformin's energy-perturbation mechanism can be leveraged in cancer cells when their mitochondrial metabolism is restored by depleting BACH1; this combination approach identifies tumor cells with high BACH1 expression as a potential biomarker-selected population for future investigation. Metformin's suppression of mTORC1 through AMPK activation, which provides a separate rationale for cancer repurposing through the PI3K-mTOR-linked growth-signaling pathway, is described in the AMPK and mTOR section above. All BACH1 findings are from preclinical cell-line and patient-derived xenograft experiments and do not establish clinical benefit in any cancer; whether metformin reaches concentrations sufficient to inhibit complex I in solid tumors at therapeutic doses in humans has not been established.

guides.description: How metformin works, its investigated benefits across infections, cancer, neurological conditions and physical function, and its safety.

sections.label: Overview
sections.title: What is metformin?
sections.paragraph: Metformin is an oral glucose-lowering medicine in the biguanide class. In the United States, immediate-release metformin tablets are approved alongside diet and exercise for type 2 diabetes in adults and children aged 10 years and older. It reduces the liver’s glucose production and improves the body’s response to insulin; those established uses are distinct from the repurposing investigations discussed here. Researchers are studying whether its effects on metabolism, cellular energy sensing and inflammatory pathways can help in acute COVID-19 and Long COVID, Parkinson’s disease, cognition in schizophrenia, and age-related loss of muscle function. Cancer research includes trials in prostate, lung, breast and pancreatic cancer, studies of recurrent colorectal adenomas after polyp removal, and laboratory work in multiple myeloma. The findings vary by condition and outcome: promising biological effects have often failed to translate into clinical benefit, and preventing a condition, treating established disease and changing a laboratory marker are different questions.

sections.label: Benefits
sections.paragraph: The benefits being investigated include reducing Long COVID risk, improving cognition in schizophrenia, preserving physical function in older adults and improving Parkinson’s symptoms. A small schizophrenia trial reported improved cognitive-test scores with metformin, while the Parkinson’s pilot and the MET-PREVENT sarcopenia trial did not demonstrate improvements in their main clinical outcomes. For Long COVID, COVID-OUT reported a prevention signal, although a correction notice and inconsistent control percentages complicate interpretation; ACTIV-6 did not meet its primary efficacy threshold, and a separate trial found no improved recovery after symptoms were established. Cancer trials have generally not demonstrated the hoped-for treatment benefits; a separate colorectal study found fewer recurrent adenomas after polyp removal, which is a prevention outcome.

questions.question: Does metformin improve symptoms of Parkinson’s disease?
questions.answer: A three-month pilot randomized 60 people to metformin or placebo alongside levodopa/carbidopa. Clinical scores improved within the metformin group, but the comparison between groups did not show a statistically significant benefit on the total Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale. The trial was small, used a per-protocol analysis and was too short to establish whether metformin slows disease progression.

questions.question: What has the schizophrenia research found about cognition?
questions.answer: In a 72-person open-label randomized trial, adding metformin to antipsychotic treatment improved the composite cognitive-test score by an estimated 3.43 points more than antipsychotics alone after 24 weeks (95% CI 1.83–5.02). The participants were predominantly young adults, 59 completed follow-up, and the study lacked a placebo group; larger blinded studies are needed to confirm the size and practical importance of this effect. A later analysis of the same trial linked changes in metabolites and hippocampal connectivity with cognitive changes.

questions.question: Does metformin improve muscle strength or physical function?
questions.answer: The 2025 MET-PREVENT trial randomized 72 older adults with probable sarcopenia and prefrailty or frailty to metformin or placebo for four months. It found no walking-speed benefit: the adjusted difference was 0.001 m/s (95% CI −0.06 to 0.06), and metformin was poorly tolerated in this population. The 2023 review described inconsistent results: some research suggested faster walking, but strength outcomes were not consistently improved and exercise adaptations could be reduced. In the MASTERS trial, adding metformin to resistance training reduced muscle growth in healthy older adults; the difference in strength gains was not statistically significant.

questions.question: Does taking metformin during COVID-19 prevent Long COVID?
questions.answer: COVID-OUT reported fewer later clinician-diagnosed cases when treatment began during acute infection, but the estimate remains provisional because the report contains inconsistent control percentages and has a published correction. ACTIV-6 examined symptoms attributed to COVID-19 or death at six months and did not meet its prespecified threshold for benefit. The trials enrolled different populations and used different outcomes, leaving uncertainty about how much prevention benefit metformin provides.

A separate metformin-and-fluvoxamine fatigue report was retracted and republished; its original findings cannot serve as reliable evidence of metformin benefit.

sections.label: Safety
sections.paragraph: Metformin commonly causes diarrhoea, nausea and abdominal discomfort; longer use can lower vitamin B12. Its major serious risk is lactic acidosis, particularly with impaired kidney function, hypoxia, liver disease or excessive alcohol intake.

sections.label: Interactions

sections.label: Dosing
sections.title: What schedules have repurposing trials tested?
sections.paragraph: The COVID-OUT and ACTIV-6 prevention trials tested a 14-day course of immediate-release metformin, increasing to 1,500 mg daily. The Parkinson’s pilot used 500 mg twice daily for three months, while the schizophrenia trial used up to 1,500 mg daily for 24 weeks. These studies tested different treatment schedules for different conditions; they did not establish one repurposing dose or demonstrate equivalent outcomes with extended-release metformin.

questions.question: What are the labeled starting dose and titration schedule for immediate-release metformin?
questions.answer: The U.S. prescribing information for immediate-release metformin tablets lists a starting dose of 500 mg twice daily or 850 mg once daily, taken with meals. The dose is increased by 500 mg each week or by 850 mg every two weeks, based on glycemic control and tolerability, up to a maximum of 2,550 mg per day in divided doses. The label notes that doses above 2,000 mg per day may be better tolerated when divided into three doses taken with meals. These are the labeled regimens for type 2 diabetes; repurposing trials used their own schedules.

questions.question: What is the labeled starting dose and maximum for extended-release metformin?
questions.answer: The U.S. prescribing information for extended-release metformin tablets recommends starting at 500 mg once daily with the evening meal. The dose is increased by 500 mg each week based on glycemic control and tolerability, up to a maximum of 2,000 mg once daily with the evening meal. The label states that patients already receiving immediate-release metformin may switch to the same total daily dose as extended-release taken once daily. The extended-release label does not include a pediatric dosing section.

questions.question: Do immediate-release and extended-release metformin have the same efficacy and tolerability?
questions.answer: A 2021 systematic review and meta-analysis of nine randomized controlled trials in 2,609 adults with type 2 diabetes found that extended-release metformin produced statistically worse but likely clinically similar HbA1c lowering compared with immediate-release. Extended-release reduced dyspepsia relative to immediate-release but did not significantly reduce overall gastrointestinal intolerance, including diarrhea, abdominal discomfort, and nausea. The U.S. prescribing information for each formulation describes its own dosing regimen and does not assert equivalent glycemic efficacy across formulations.

questions.question: How should metformin dosing be adjusted based on kidney function?
questions.answer: Both the immediate-release and extended-release U.S. prescribing information require assessment of kidney function (eGFR) before starting metformin and periodically during treatment. Starting metformin is not recommended when eGFR is 30 to 45 mL/min/1.73 m2; metformin is contraindicated and should be discontinued when eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73 m2. A 2014 systematic review in JAMA of metformin in type 2 diabetes and kidney disease found that lactate concentrations are not substantially increased at eGFR values of 30 to 60 mL/min/1.73 m2, and concluded that cautious use with dose monitoring is warranted in mild-to-moderate chronic kidney disease.

sections.paragraph: FDA-approved generic medicines must match the reference product’s active ingredient, strength, dosage form and route, and demonstrate bioequivalence. Release formulation also matters: the Long COVID prevention trials described here used immediate-release metformin and did not compare it with an extended-release product.

sections.label: Status
sections.paragraph: The U.S. prescribing information lists metformin as an adjunct to diet and exercise for type 2 diabetes in adults and children aged 10 years and older. sections.label: Evidence
sections.paragraph: The human evidence spans prevention, treatment and physical or cognitive function, with different populations, comparators and follow-up periods. Several cancer trials did not demonstrate the expected clinical benefit; adenoma recurrence after polyp removal is a separate prevention outcome. The schizophrenia metabolite and imaging report analyzes the same trial as the earlier cognitive report, so it does not add a second independent trial. Cell and mouse findings explain biological rationale but cannot establish patient benefit. COVID-OUT has a published correction notice and conflicting control-group percentages in the available report. Its long-term diagnosis estimate should be read with that qualification. The original REVIVE fatigue report has a notice of retraction and republication; its original results are not used as evidence of benefit.

faqs.question: Do immediate-release and extended-release metformin have the same evidence for Long COVID?
faqs.answer: The prevention trials used immediate-release metformin. They did not compare release formulations, so their results do not establish equal Long COVID outcomes for an extended-release product.

faqs.question: Is a short course during COVID-19 the same as treating established Long COVID?
faqs.answer: No. Prevention trials start treatment during the acute infection and measure later illness, whereas the South Korean treatment trial enrolled people who already had persistent symptoms.

faqs.question: Is metformin approved for the repurposing uses on this page?
faqs.answer: The cited U.S. tablet label lists type 2 diabetes as the approved indication. The cancer, COVID-19, neurological and muscle-function investigations on this page do not add approved indications to that label.

faqs.question: Does a plausible mechanism mean metformin works for that condition?
faqs.answer: No. MA.32 illustrates the distinction: metformin changed metabolic factors, but did not improve invasive disease-free survival in the clinical report. A pathway finding, a biomarker change and a patient outcome answer different questions.

faqs.question: Does the colorectal finding mean metformin treats colorectal cancer?
faqs.answer: The cited trial tested recurrent adenomas and polyps after their removal. Its prevention finding does not establish that metformin treats established colorectal cancer or improves cancer survival.
